title: Organs, guitars and drums

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymnals, the book in the pew. Your line was theology in song. What song got stuck in your head, and what was it teaching? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

The first note comes up through the floor before it reaches your ears. A low hum in the soles of your shoes, then the whole stone room fills with sound from a wall of metal pipes. That's one Sunday morning. Across town, a drummer clicks his sticks together, one, two, three, four, and a guitar and a bass come in under a screen of lyrics. In a third church, there's no instrument at all. A single voice sings a line, and the room answers it. Pipes, a drum kit, one voice with nothing under it. Ask in any of those rooms what's going on, and you may hear the same answer: praising God with what they have. Today: organs, guitars and drums.

Start at the end of the book of Psalms. Psalm one hundred fifty is a list of instruments, one after another, and in the King James Bible it says: "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Organs, right there in the Psalms. But some readers take the Hebrew word behind it as a simple pipe, nothing like a cathedral organ with pedals. The psalm wasn't describing one sound. It was gathering every sound it knew. Next, the new. Another psalm says: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise." A new song, played with skill, and loudly. Churches with guitars, drums and keyboards often point to lines like that. So do churches with pipe organs, which were once new themselves. Each generation brings the instruments it has. Then, the churches that use none. Orthodox churches traditionally sing their services without instruments, and so do some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ. They read the New Testament's words about worship, like Paul's letter to the Ephesians: "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." For them, the human voice is the instrument God made. Those churches and the ones with organs or drums each have reasons, and each takes them seriously. Last, the final verse of that list psalm. After trumpet, harp, strings, pipes and two kinds of cymbal, the psalm doesn't end on an instrument. It ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Before any pipe or string, there's breath. Every instrument on the list depends on it, and every person has it.

Here's the practice: listen to a church instrument. If you can, play a recording of an organ, a gospel band, or a hymn with guitar, whichever you can find. Settle, and breathe, and listen for two minutes without doing anything else. Notice where the sound sits in your body: chest, feet, throat. If you can't play anything, listen to your own breathing instead, the instrument the psalm ends on. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without adding any words. If you don't, just listen, all the way to the end. The bell holds the time.
Organs. The pipes in old churches, a word the King James Psalms already used, and a reminder that churches praise with the sounds they have.

Your line: every instrument praise. This week ran from colors of the year, incense and candles to the cross, icons, hymnals and now organs: faith you can see, smell and hear. Today, notice one ordinary sound and hear it as part of the psalm's long list. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

notes: Editor pass: the lexical claim about the Hebrew behind 'organs' is now 'some readers take it as a pipe' (no 'probably' or 'uncertain' as fact), Orthodox unaccompanied singing is 'traditionally', and the hook's 'three rooms, three sounds' line (a device used on days 1356 and 1358) was rewritten.

The Hebrew ugav (עוּגָב) in Psalm 150:4, rendered 'organs' in the KJV, is generally taken as a pipe or flute; the lesson says 'probably' and 'uncertain'. Confirm, and confirm the Hebrew spelling and pronunciation.
'Organs' is the index word (title head); the lesson spans organs, guitars and drums as the title does.
'Pipe organs, which were once new themselves' is a general historical remark without a date; confirm acceptable.
Orthodox churches singing unaccompanied, and the Churches of Christ as an example of Protestant a cappella worship: confirm fair description.
Week end (days 1359–1365): the carry names the week's topics.
'Two kinds of cymbal' paraphrases Psalm 150:5 ('loud cymbals', 'high sounding cymbals').
